_readme: THE PERSONAL-DATA INVENTORY — [pipeline K-8] Private/requirements/ (was pipeline/08-compliance-legal.md, folded into the JSON spec 2026-08-15)
One row for every place this factory can put data: every table any migration creates, every D1
database, KV namespace and R2 bucket any wrangler config binds, and every KV binding a Cloudflare
Pages Function reaches. What each holds, how long it is kept, what code writes it, and — where it
holds anything about a person — the SENTENCE ON THE PUBLISHED PAGE that discloses it.
🔴 THE ROW SET MUST EQUAL THE DERIVED STORE SET, BOTH DIRECTIONS, and the second direction is the
one that matters. `a store with no row` catches data arriving undisclosed. `a row with no store`
is what stops this file becoming a wish-list: without it, a table could be renamed, the row would
keep describing the old name, and the inventory would go on looking complete while describing a
schema that no longer exists.
DERIVED, NOT LISTED. The right-hand side is computed from the tree on every run:
· every CREATE TABLE in services/*/migrations/*.sql, with COMMENTS AND STRING LITERALS STRIPPED
first — a table name inside a comment is not a table, and this repo has already shipped a guard
that matched the comment explaining why a binding did NOT exist;
· every d1_databases / kv_namespaces / r2_buckets entry in EVERY wrangler config in the repo,
PARSED as JSONC rather than grepped. ⚠️ Repo-wide on purpose: assert-clone-contract.mjs reads
only services/<app>-api/wrangler.jsonc, so services/subscriptiontracker-api is invisible to it. Borrowing
that walk would have inherited the blind spot and reported full coverage of a subset;
· every KV binding a Pages Function calls (`env.SIGNUPS.put(...)`). These are bound in the
Cloudflare dashboard and appear in NO wrangler config, so a wrangler-only walk would miss the
one store in this repository that holds a plain email address.
⚠️ WHAT IS PUBLIC HERE. This is a public repository and this file describes SHAPE, never CONTENT: a
store exists, it holds this CATEGORY of data, it is written by this file, it is kept for this long.
No row contains a person's data, an identifier, a key, or a database id. See tooling/legal/README.md.
🔴 AND EVERY TABLE CARRIES AN ERASURE STORY, because a delete route that silently misses rows is
worse than no delete route: the user is told their data is gone and stops asking. The erasure route
(services/platform/src/routes/account.ts) DERIVES the tables it empties from the schema — every table
with a `user_id` column — which is right, and has one consequence nobody had written down: a table
holding personal data WITHOUT such a column is invisible to it, and the route still answers ok:true.
`provider_notifications` was exactly that table until migration 0006. So `erasure` is now required on
every d1-table row and every row that holds personal data, its `kind` is CHECKED AGAINST THE PARSED
SCHEMA (a `purge` row whose table has no `user_id` fails; a `pseudonymous` row whose table GROWS one
fails, because the declaration has become false), and a store no route can reach PRINTS every run
with the thing that blocks it named. The behaviour behind the declaration is proven separately, by
services/platform/test/erasure-reach.test.ts, which plants a row in every table this file names,
runs the REAL route against the REAL migrations, and asserts the erased user's id survives in no
column of any table.
RETENTION IS A DECLARATION, AND `undecided` IS AN HONEST ONE. Every row carries `retention`.
`ttl` states the bound and the code that sets it. `keep` requires a written reason. `undecided`
requires an ownerItem and PRINTS on every run — because choosing how long to keep a real person's
data is a legal and business decision, not something an agent should quietly pick a number for. The
guard fails a row with NO retention field at all; it never invents one.
Enforced by tooling/ci/assert-data-inventory.mjs. COVERAGE LOST when any of the three walks
under-reaches the floors in `derivation` below.

_why: THE FLOORS ARE A RELATIONSHIP, NOT A GUESS. Each is the count measured on the tree the day this
file landed, and a walk that finds FEWER has broken rather than shrunk — a migration directory
that stops being found makes every 'is this table declared?' question vacuously true.
They are also the mutation targets: deleting one migration file is COVERAGE LOST, not a pass.
_whyErasureFloor: How many rows must actually have their erasure story CHECKED AGAINST THE SCHEMA. Measured on the
tree the day the limb landed (13 d1-table rows + the one Pages KV namespace that holds a plain
email address). A run that checks fewer has stopped reaching rows, and 'every table has an erasure
story' would range over a subset while printing ok — the exact shape check-migrations.mjs failed in
silently when it dropped from 5 files to 4.

retentionKinds._why: The vocabulary rows are validated against, declared in the register rather than in the guard so that renaming a kind out from under the rows using it fails.
retentionKinds.ttl: the store expires the record itself, and the row names the code that sets the expiry.
retentionKinds.swept: a DECLARED period that a job of ours enforces, because the store has no expiry of its own. Requires a `periodDays` and a `sweptBy` naming the code that deletes. ⚠️ DISTINCT FROM `ttl` ON PURPOSE: `ttl` says the STORE forgets, which is a property of the substrate and survives our code being wrong or absent; `swept` says WE forget, which holds only while a scheduled job keeps running. D1 has no TTL, so every D1 period is this kind — and calling it `ttl` would claim a durability guarantee the substrate does not give. Added 2026-08-12 with the events rollup: `events` and `provider_notifications` had been sitting at `undecided` since before [ADR 045] locked 400 and 730, so this file was still printing RETENTION UNDECIDED and asking the owner for numbers they had already given.
retentionKinds.keep: kept until deliberately deleted. Requires a written reason — 'we might want it' is not one.
retentionKinds.undecided: nobody has decided yet. Requires an ownerItem, and PRINTS every run so it cannot become permanent by being invisible.
retentionKinds.derived: holds no record of its own; its lifetime is the lifetime of the rows inside it (a database, not a table).

_why: The vocabulary lives here, not in the guard, for the same reason `retentionKinds` does: renaming a
kind out from under the rows using it must FAIL rather than quietly mean nothing.
🔴 EVERY KIND IS CHECKED AGAINST THE PARSED SCHEMA, not taken on trust. That is what makes this a
RELATIONSHIP rather than a second wish-list: `purge` asserts the column the route derives from is
really there, and `pseudonymous` / `no-personal-data` assert that no user-shaped column is — so a
migration that adds `user_id` to `events` tomorrow turns the declaration false and the build red,
instead of leaving a row that says 'unreachable' about a table that is now reachable.
erasureKinds.purge: the table carries a column literally called `user_id`, so the schema-derived sweep in the named `route` DELETEs this person's rows. Checked: the column must exist in the migrations.
erasureKinds.unlink: the row is NOT this person's, but a `*_user_id` column REFERENCES them; the sweep NULLs that column so no dangling identifier of an erased person survives. Requires `column`. Checked: the column must exist and must end in `_user_id`.
erasureKinds.pseudonymous: nothing in the table resolves to an account, so an erasure request cannot address it and 'zero rows for this user' is vacuously true. Requires a written reason. Checked: the table must carry NO user-shaped column — the day one is added this declaration is false and the guard says so.
erasureKinds.completion-ledger: ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 081]. The table records an erasure IN PROGRESS — it names a person under a deliberately NEUTRAL column (`column`, e.g. `subject_ref`) that the schema-derived sweep cannot see, BECAUSE a `user_id`-named ledger would be deleted by the very erasure it records. Its rows are deleted by the named `deletedBy` code when that erasure completes. Checked: the column exists and is NOT user-shaped (neither `user_id` nor `*_user_id`), and `deletedBy` is a file.
erasureKinds.no-personal-data: the table holds nothing about a person, so there is nothing to erase. Requires personalData:false. Checked the same way as `pseudonymous`.
erasureKinds.purge-by-verified-email: ⏱ 2026-09-15 · [ADR 087]. The table is keyed by an EMAIL ADDRESS, not by an account, so the schema-derived sweep cannot address it — but the erasure route reaches it for a person who HAS an account: before the identity is deleted it reads the account from the identity provider and deletes the rows whose `column` equals that account's address, ONLY when the provider says the address is CONFIRMED (an unconfirmed address would let anyone remove someone else's row). Requires `column`, `route` and `verifiedBy` (the file that holds the confirmed-address delete). Checked here: the column exists and is NOT user-shaped, both files exist. Checked by tooling/ci/assert-erasure-reach.mjs: `verifiedBy` deletes from this table on this column only after reading `email_confirmed_at`, and every caller of the identity delete calls that purge first. A person with no account (or no confirmed address) is not reached by the route; `blockedBy` says how they are served.
erasureKinds.no-route: 🔴 A STORE HOLDING PERSONAL DATA THAT NO DEPLOYED ERASURE ROUTE REACHES. Requires `blockedBy` naming what stops it. PRINTS on every run rather than failing the build — the fix is an architecture or owner decision, and a guard that reddens main on work nobody can do today is a guard somebody switches off.

stores.name: platform_db
stores.holds: The shared portfolio database. Holds no rows of its own; its tables do.

retention.reason: A database is a container. Every table in it carries its own row below.

stores.note: 🔴 ONE DATABASE FOR THE WHOLE PORTFOLIO. services/platform is its sole migrations applier, which is why check-migrations.mjs treats a destructive statement here as a portfolio-wide outage rather than one app's problem.

stores.name: subscriptiontracker_db
stores.holds: Subly's own database. Holds no rows of its own; its tables do.

retention.reason: A container. See the table rows below.

stores.name: {{app_id}}_db
stores.holds: The per-app database a BACKEND stamp creates. A template, not a live store — the name is a mustache placeholder and resolves per stamped app.

retention.reason: A container, and a template of one. Each stamped app inherits the table rows its own migrations create.

stores.note: Included deliberately rather than filtered out as 'just a template'. It is the binding every future app will have, and an inventory that skips the brick is an inventory that is wrong the day app number two ships.

stores.name: entitlements
stores.holds: One row per (user, app, entitlement): what a person has paid for. Keyed on a store/aggregator user id, not on a name or an email.

retention.reason: An entitlement is the record of what somebody bought and is entitled to keep using. Deleting it deletes their purchase. It is retained for as long as the account exists, and erasure is [pipeline K-7]'s route — DELETE /v1/account, which landed with [4]B-5 and reaches this table through its `user_id` column.

erasure.reason: Keyed (user_id, app_id, entitlement). The account is gone, so the entitlement it granted is gone with it — and master §0.1 G2 names this table specifically.

stores.name: provider_notifications
stores.holds: 🔴 THE ONE TABLE IN platform_db THAT IS NOT PSEUDONYMOUS, and it is named as such rather than discovered. Every merchant-of-record notification, stored VERBATIM — byte for byte, exactly as it arrived and exactly as it was signed. Whatever the provider put in it is therefore in it, which for a subscription event includes the buyer's name, email address and billing country. That is inherent in 'recorded verbatim' ([pipeline 5]M-2): a re-serialised or redacted copy is a different byte string and can never be re-verified against the signature that came with it, so a redacted store is a store that cannot prove what it received. It carries NO anon_id, so no code path can pair a payer with a pseudonymous install ([ADR 020]:21).

retention.sweptBy: services/platform/src/scheduled.ts — the `provider_notifications` limb of `retentionSweep`, PROVIDER_NOTIFICATIONS_RETENTION_DAYS. 🔴 IT DELETES ONLY WHERE `derived_at IS NOT NULL AND derive_error IS NULL`, and that predicate is a LEGAL CONDITION, not an optimisation: if derivation never resolved, no derived record exists, the raw payload IS the book of account by function, and it inherits CGST s.36 (~2,698 days). The sweep's legality is a property of that predicate, not of the period.
retention.reason: 🔒 LOCKED 730 DAYS (2 years) by [ADR 045]. ⚠️ THE OBVIOUS JUSTIFICATION IS FALSE AND IS NOT USED: 'we need it to fight chargebacks' does not survive Paddle's own documentation — Paddle is merchant of record, the dispute is raised against Paddle, its help centre says seller evidence is 'not required or accepted', and it retains the transaction for 5 years. The real reasons are that Paddle will NOT replay a notification older than 90 days, so from day 91 ours is the sole surviving copy; and that Visa's outer dispute window is 540 days, which 730 clears with margin. 📌 THIS ROW READ `undecided` / O-3 until 2026-08-12 — see the note on `table:platform_db.events`; both were locked by ADR 045 on 2026-08-12 and neither row was updated, so this file printed two RETENTION UNDECIDED lines for decisions that had already been made.

erasure.reason: 🔴 THE GAP THIS FILE WAS EXTENDED TO CLOSE. Until services/platform/migrations/0006_erasure_reach.sql this table carried NO `user_id`, so the schema-derived sweep could not see it — a person could ask to be erased, be told they were, and have their name and email address still sitting in the verbatim payload. 0006 adds the column and services/platform/src/lib/mor/store.ts stamps it at DERIVE time (the row is written before it is interpreted, so that is the first moment the account is known), which puts the table inside the sweep with no edit to the route.

unverified.question: Whether a merchant-of-record payment notification carries a STATUTORY RETENTION BASIS (tax, accounting, or consumer-law) that would override erasure for this row, and for how long.
unverified.status: UNVERIFIED — no primary source for such an obligation could be read from this environment, and none is invented here. The default shipped is to PURGE, because honouring the published promise needs no justification while RETAINING a person's data does. Nothing writes to this table yet (OWNER_QUEUE A-1), so the decision is still free; it stops being free at the first payment.

stores.note: ⚠️ THE PUBLISHED SENTENCE QUOTED ABOVE IS TRUE AND INCOMPLETE. It tells a reader the transaction is processed by a payment processor; it does not tell them we KEEP A COPY of what that processor sent us about them. stores.name: provider_accounts
stores.holds: The link between a provider's subscription id and one of our account ids, written once, on the first notification that provably carries both ([pipeline 5]M-7). Four columns and two timestamps; no name, no email, no payment detail. It exists because whether checkout metadata propagates onto RENEWAL transactions is a vendor fact this repo could not establish from a primary source, and a renewal that cannot be attributed is a paying customer who silently loses access.

retention.reason: It is the answer to 'why do we believe this subscription belongs to this account', and it is needed for as long as the subscription can renew, lapse or be refunded — i.e. for the life of the account. It is ERASED WITH THE ACCOUNT and needs no special handling to be: the shared erasure route derives its table set from the schema (every table carrying a `user_id` column), so this table joined that set the moment it was created, with no edit to the route.

erasure.reason: The row IS the link between a person and a subscription. When the person is erased the link has nothing left to join, and leaving it would keep their account id in the database after the account is gone.

stores.name: ai_accounts
stores.holds: ⏱ 2026-10-02 · T17 (train-st-ai-customer-pays). One row per (account, app) that used or bought paid AI: the paid pack credits left, the monthly allowance used and its month, and the version and time of the AI disclosure the user acknowledged. No content: no prompt, image, e-mail or model answer is ever stored.

retention.reason: A credit balance is what the customer paid for and the opt-in is the record that they agreed to the AI disclosure; both are needed for as long as the account exists. ERASED WITH THE ACCOUNT by construction: the column is spelled `user_id`, and the shared erasure route derives the tables it empties from the schema.

erasure.reason: The row is the person's: their balance and their consent. Erasing the account leaves nothing for it to describe.

stores.name: ai_ledger
stores.holds: ⏱ 2026-10-02 · T17 (train-st-ai-customer-pays). One row per paid AI call (the feature, the model, the credit source, tokens in and out and the USD it cost at the model's own prices) and one per verified pack purchase (the rail and its purchase reference, credits granted, revoked on refund). No content: the request body is never persisted.

retention.reason: The ledger explains a customer's balance and is what the global daily spend circuit-breaker sums; it is kept for the life of the account. ERASED WITH THE ACCOUNT by construction: the column is spelled `user_id`.

erasure.reason: Every row names the person's account. When the account is erased the ledger has nobody left to explain a balance to.

stores.name: refund_requests
stores.holds: ⏱ 2026-10-02 · refund-finish (MF-5). One row per in-window refund a signed-in user asked for: our account id, the app, the rail and its purchase reference, the request's idempotency key, when the charge happened (the rail's own clock), when it was asked, and the rail's refund reference once carried out — or why it was not. References only: no card, UPI or bank detail.

retention.reason: A refund is a money event a dispute, a chargeback or an audit can ask about for as long as the account exists, and the row is what stops one payment being refunded twice. ERASED WITH THE ACCOUNT by construction: the column is spelled `user_id`.

erasure.reason: The row is the person's request. When the account is erased the request has nobody left to answer to.

stores.name: provider_payment_links
stores.holds: ⏱ 2026-10-02 · PR #1149 ruling item 2 (O-RAZORPAY-CHECKOUT-ADAPTER). One row per subscription charge on a rail whose refunds and disputes name a PAYMENT rather than a subscription (Razorpay): the rail's payment id, the subscription id it charged, our account id when the charge resolved one, the money world, and the notification that carried both ids. Written once, first link wins, on the signed `subscription.charged`, so a later refund or chargeback of that payment resolves its subscription without trusting the payment entity's own fields. No name, no email, no payment detail.

retention.reason: It is the answer to 'which subscription does this refunded or disputed payment belong to', and a refund or chargeback can arrive for as long as the subscription's payments can be reversed — i.e. for the life of the account. It is ERASED WITH THE ACCOUNT by construction: the column is spelled `user_id`, and the shared erasure route derives the tables it empties from the schema.

erasure.reason: The row links a person's payment to their subscription. When the person is erased the link has nothing left to resolve to (provider_accounts goes with them), and keeping it would keep their account id after the account is gone. A row written with no account (an unclaimed charge) carries no user id and is not theirs to erase.

stores.name: unclaimed_payments
stores.holds: Money that arrived and could not be attributed to an account ([pipeline 5]M-7) — the alternative to the legacy route's acknowledge-and-discard, which left the payer's only record with the provider. The buyer's email is stored as a SHA-256 HEX DIGEST, never as an address: the claim-on-first-signin lookup is an exact match, which a hash serves exactly as well, so the queryable column is not a list of customers' email addresses. Also the provider's own ids, for a support lookup in their dashboard.

retention.reason: A row here is the evidence that somebody paid and we could not find them; deleting it destroys the only thing that could ever resolve their support ticket, and keeping it forever means holding a pseudonymised identifier for a person who may never appear. The ROW is not erased; the LINK to the erased person is — see `erasure` below.

erasure.reason: 🔴 THE QUESTION 0004 DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN, ANSWERED — AND ANSWERED THE WAY THAT DESTROYS NOTHING. The row is the record of money that arrived and could not be attributed: deleting it removes the only thing that could ever resolve that payer's support ticket, so it is kept. But `claimed_user_id` is the ERASED PERSON'S ACCOUNT ID, and a row still addressable by the identifier of someone who asked to be forgotten is not erased. So the route NULLs the column and keeps the row. The rule is derived from the schema, not from a list: `user_id` means the row IS theirs (delete it), `*_user_id` means the row REFERENCES them (null it), so a future `linked_user_id` is covered the day it is created. ⚠️ `claimed_at` is deliberately LEFT SET — 'this payment was claimed' stays true and is what stops it being claimed twice; what is erased is WHO. ⚠️ HONEST RESIDUE: `customer_email_hash` is a SHA-256 of an email address and is NOT anonymous — it is pseudonymised, and the same person hashing to the same value is the whole point of the lookup. Unlinking does not remove it, and no claim is made here that it does; whether an erasure should also clear the hash on an unclaimed row is part of the same undecided retention question above.

disclosure.quote: if you buy something, the transaction is processed by the relevant app store or by our payment processor

export.reason: The row is NOT the person's: it references them through a `*_user_id` column and holds the buyer's address only as a SHA-256 digest. An access request that asks about a payment is answered by hand from this row (docs/ops/privacy-requests.md), never by a bulk export of other people's unattributed money.

stores.name: cancellation_requests
stores.holds: One row per time a user pressed Cancel ([pipeline 5]M-9, ROSCA). It holds WHO asked (the Supabase `sub`), for which app, in which money world, and which provider subscription it was about — copied at request time rather than joined, because the entitlement row can be revoked and rewritten afterwards and this record has to keep saying what the user was cancelling. It holds no name, no email and no payment detail. 🔴 IT EXISTS BECAUSE OF A GAP THE USER WOULD OTHERWISE FALL INTO: only the merchant of record can actually stop a subscription, so between 'I pressed cancel' and 'the rail acted' the ONLY evidence that they asked is what we wrote down. Without it, a cancellation the provider dropped is indistinguishable from one nobody requested, and the person still being billed is the one who has to prove otherwise.

retention.reason: KEPT until the account is erased, and the reason it is kept is the whole point of the table: it is the only evidence the user asked. It joins the erasure set BY CONSTRUCTION: the column is spelled `user_id`, and the shared erasure route (services/platform/src/routes/account.ts) derives the tables it empties from the schema, so this is emptied with no edit to the route. That was verified rather than assumed — adding the table turned services/platform/test/auth.test.ts red on its 'an empty derivation is a refusal' fixture, which is the derivation working. (Contrast `unclaimed_payments.claimed_user_id`, which is UNLINKED rather than deleted for the reason recorded above.)

erasure.reason: A cancellation request IS a record about a person and goes when they do. The evidentiary value it exists for — 'the user asked three times and nothing happened' — is value to THAT user; once the account is erased there is nobody it could be produced for.

stores.name: content_reports
stores.holds: One row per in-app report of AI-generated content (O-PLAY-AI-CONTENT-REPORTING; Google Play AI-Generated Content policy, support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13985936). It holds WHO reported (the Supabase `sub`, from the verified JWT), for which app, a reason from a closed set, a reference to and/or an excerpt of the generated content (≤2000 chars), and an optional note the user typed (≤1000 chars) — plus `status` for moderation and `notified_at` for the support notice. It holds no name and no email address. The note is free text a person wrote, so it is treated as personal data in full. No app writes to it today: only an app that generates content with AI shows the report control.

retention.reason: 400 days from `created_at`, enforced by the platform Worker's nightly `retentionSweep` (CONTENT_REPORTS_RETENTION_DAYS) — the platform's period for personal data, clearing the DPDP Rules 2025 Rule 8(3) one-year floor that 365 misses across a 29 February ([ADR 045] §9). Kept that long so repeated reports against the same generated content can be seen and acted on, which is what Play asks developers to use reports for. `swept`, not `ttl`: D1 has no expiry.

erasure.reason: A report is a record about the person who filed it, and the note is their words; it goes when they do. The column is spelled `user_id` ON PURPOSE (0013_content_reports.sql): the shared erasure walk DELETES the row rather than NULLing a `*_user_id` reference and keeping the text. Verified rather than assumed — adding the table turned services/platform/test/auth.test.ts's empty-derivation fixture and erasure-derivation.test.ts's pinned set red.

disclosure.quote: when you contact support, send feedback, or (in apps that offer accounts) create an account

stores.name: ext_codes
stores.holds: ⏱ 2026-09-24 · O-EXTENSION-ACCOUNT-CHECK-UNBUILT. One row per one-time code minted when a signed-in user connects the browser extension on https://nikatru.com/ext/connect: SHA-256 of the code (the code itself is never stored), WHO minted it (the Supabase `sub`, from the verified JWT), the product (`fullshot`), the store channel, the exact redirect_uri the code may be delivered to, the PKCE S256 challenge, and `created_at` / `expires_at` / `used_at`. A code lives 120 seconds and is single-use. It holds no name and no email address. ⏱ 2026-09-30 · EXA-11: plus `auth_at` (0021_ext_link_floor.sql), when the minting session started, copied to the link at exchange.

retention.reason: One day past `expires_at`, enforced by the platform Worker's nightly `retentionSweep` (EXT_CODES_RETENTION_DAYS) — the design's 24 hours after expiry. After `expires_at` a code can never be exchanged, so the row is only a record that a sign-in was attempted; the day keeps it readable the morning after a failed connect. The cutoff is on `expires_at`, so an unexpired code is never swept. `swept`, not `ttl`: D1 has no expiry.

erasure.reason: A code is a record of the account that minted it. The column is spelled `user_id` ON PURPOSE (0017_ext_devices.sql): the shared erasure walk DELETES the row. Verified rather than assumed — adding the table turned services/platform/test/auth.test.ts's empty-derivation fixture and erasure-derivation.test.ts's pinned set red.

disclosure.quote: when you contact support, send feedback, or (in apps that offer accounts) create an account

stores.name: ext_devices
stores.holds: ⏱ 2026-09-24 · O-EXTENSION-ACCOUNT-CHECK-UNBUILT. One row per browser that has linked the extension to an account: a random link id (`link_id`), the Supabase `sub`, the product (`fullshot`), the store channel, SHA-256 of the device credential (the credential is returned once to the extension and never stored), `created_at`, `last_seen_at` (at most once per UTC day) and `revoked_at`. The credential can read that one product's entitlement and revoke itself, nothing else. It holds no name and no email address. ⏱ 2026-09-30 · EXA-11: plus `auth_at` (0021_ext_link_floor.sql) — when the Supabase session that minted the link started, compared against the account's link floor.

retention.reason: ⏱ 2026-09-25, amended 2026-09-30 (EXA-11). Thirty days after `revoked_at`, OR thirty days after the link's lifetime ended, enforced by the platform Worker's nightly `retentionSweep` (EXT_DEVICES_RETENTION_DAYS). Since 2026-09-30 the credential HAS a lifetime (services/platform/src/lib/ext-links.ts: 30 days unused, 180 days at most), so a never-revoked row is swept 30 days after it expired — a browser that was uninstalled never comes back to have it stamped revoked. Inside its lifetime a never-revoked row is a live credential and is not swept. It also ends when the account is erased. A revoked, expired or floored row answers 401 from that moment, and a deleted row answers the same 401. `swept`, not `ttl`: D1 has no expiry.

retention.sweptBy: services/platform/src/scheduled.ts — the `events_daily` limb of `retentionSweep`, EVENTS_DAILY_RETENTION_DAYS. retention.reason: 1100 days (~3 years) = 1095 + 5 days' margin, the same shape as events' 400 = 365 + 35. The floor is 1095 — three calendar years, the minimum for TWO year-over-year comparisons — and that is the first thing the raw table's 400 days cannot buy, which is the entire reason this table exists. No statutory ceiling applies: GA4's 425-day cap governs raw, event-level, device-and-geo-bearing data, and this table has none of that. DPDP s.6(1) purpose limitation still binds, and 'portfolio seasonality across three years' is a stated, bounded purpose. ⚠️ THIS IS A POLICY NUMBER, NOT A MEASUREMENT — it is the one value in the rollup increment an owner may reasonably want to move, and it is locked rather than deferred only because tooling/ops/register.json caps undeclared periods at `_maxUndeclared: 0`.

The in-app deletion control exists in BOTH trees and is asserted — the `account-deletion-works` coverage key on the brick, and tooling/ci/assert-deletion-control.mjs over apps/subscriptiontracker with no exemption ([ADR 027]) — and since 2026-08-04 that control REACHES THESE ROWS. See `erasure` below. A REMOVED subscription is SOFT-deleted first (ST-E3, `deleted_at`): hidden from every list and reminder and restorable for 30 days, then purged with its payment_history and price_change rows by services/subscriptiontracker-api/src/routes/subscriptions.ts `purgeExpired`, which runs on that user's next list.

erasure.reason:
🔴 THE GAP THIS ROW USED TO DECLARE, CLOSED 2026-08-04. Until then these four rows read `no-route`: DELETE /v1/account lived only on the shared platform Worker, which sweeps PLATFORM_DB, so a Subly user could delete their account, lose their login, and leave every subscription, budget and payment they had ever entered in a database no login could ever reach again.

THE OBJECTION THAT HELD IT UP WAS REAL AND IS ANSWERED RATHER THAN WAIVED. services/subscriptiontracker-api/src/middleware/auth.ts accepts a token signed with the shared HS256 secret when the asymmetric path fails, and an irreversible route must not sit behind a symmetric secret — one leaked environment variable would mint a token for any user of any app. So the route was NOT put behind that middleware. `erasureAuth` (same file) verifies ES256 against the PUBLIC JWKS and is not even given the environment, so the secret is out of scope by the shape of the function signature; src/index.ts mounts DELETE /v1/account behind it; and the route ADDITIONALLY refuses any request whose `tokenAssurance` is not 'asymmetric'. Two independent limbs, because a mounting is one line somebody can move in a tidy-up and a refusal inside the handler is not. Both are recorded failing inputs in services/subscriptiontracker-api/test/erasure.test.ts, which drives the REAL Worker and proves the SAME HS256 token is ACCEPTED by GET /v1/subscriptions and REFUSED here — so the refusal is about the boundary, not about an invalid token.

The table set is DERIVED from the schema (every table carrying a `user_id`), so a fifth user-owned table is covered by its own migration with no edit to the route, and an EMPTY derivation is a 503 refusal rather than a fast path.

⚠️ THIS ROUTE ERASES NOTHING BUT subscriptiontracker_db. The identity record and platform_db stay the shared Worker’s: services/platform/src/routes/account.ts relays the caller’s own bearer token to this route AFTER its service-role precondition and BEFORE it deletes the identity, so a failure here stops the erasure while the user still has a login to retry with. Ordering, not duplication — exactly one piece of code destroys the identity.
